source_review.notes: Reviewed the primary Herlihy-Wing linearizability paper and Heller et al. lazy-list paper, plus current official Oracle Java SE 26 lock, read-write-lock, and ConcurrentHashMap contracts, POSIX.1-2024 mutex behavior, Linux lockdep design, and SEI CERT lock-order guidance. All eight final destinations returned HTTP 200. Current API statements are attributed to their specifications; the chapter does not infer implementation internals or universal performance.

evidence: Checked abstract object A, concrete representation C, invariant I(C), regions R, locks L, guard map g, protection sets P, strict rank, wait-for graph, stripe function, histories, and measurement variables.
Checked that logical removal, physical unlinking, retirement, and reclamation are defined as distinct transitions.
Checked that safety, linearizability, visibility, liveness, and empirical scalability are never collapsed into one property.
notation_and_syntax.notes: The notation supports the guard, order, coupling, resize, reclamation, and evidence arguments without treating an implementation policy as a theorem.

evidence: Recomputed stripe(k)=k mod 4 for keys 0 through 7 and verified the model's ordered pair for keys 5 and 7 is [1,3].
Recomputed keys 0 through 7, eight mappings, value sum 28, distinct simultaneous owners 2, and zero held locks at completion.
Recomputed Exercise 2: keys (6,1) and (5,2) both normalize to stripe acquisition [1,2].
numerical_recomputation.notes: The 1.7-times value in a worked situation is explicitly hypothetical and rejected as sufficient production evidence; no throughput or latency is presented as measured fact.

evidence: Verified the ranked-lock contradiction: every wait edge strictly increases rank, so a cycle would imply rank(l1)<rank(l1).
Verified the linearizability outline requires conflicting effects to share exclusive protection and each success/absence/failure class to have a point inside its call interval.
Verified coupling transfers protection by acquiring the next node before releasing the current edge guard; optimistic traversal instead requires lifetime safety plus validation.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: Each derivation states its assumptions, including stable identity/rank, participating resources, target memory synchronization, and safe reference lifetime.

evidence: Reviewed identical stripes, reversed two-key calls, stale adjacency, removed/reclaimed successor, empty/head sentinels, hot stripes, exact global size, and pre-lock observations.
Reviewed insert/delete, rotation, split/merge, resize/migration, snapshot, bulk operations, close/destruction, owner death, timeout, cancellation, callbacks, and partial acquisition.
Reviewed reader/writer upgrade, nonfair starvation, optimistic livelock, priority/holder delay, false sharing, hash skew, malicious hot keys, and hidden external locks.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: The module distinguishes recoverable validation failure from abstract effects and requires explicit bounds/telemetry for retry, wait, memory, snapshot, migration, and reclamation behavior.

evidence: The executable model rejects occupied-stripe acquisition, rejects nonowner release by assertion, preserves stable modulo routing, normalizes/deduplicates pair stripes, and finishes with all locks free.
Exact model invariants check keys 0..7, sum 28, same-stripe exclusion, pair order [1,3], and complete release.
The chapter's guard-map, coupling, ranked-order, validation, resize-generation, and lifetime invariants cover local and cross-region representation obligations.
invariant_checking.notes: The state model is intentionally finite and single-process/single-interpreter; it is not evidence that a runtime mutex or production representation implements the modeled transitions.

evidence: Reviewed derivation from sequential conflict relation through guard mapping, acquisition, validation, effect, invariant restoration, linearization, release, and reclamation.
Reviewed strict-rank deadlock proof and its exclusions for callbacks, external resources, conditions, recursion, unstable ranks, starvation, and livelock.
Reviewed operation-specific reasoning for list insert/remove/contains, two-key operations, tree rotations, hash resize, exact aggregates, weak iteration, and atomic snapshots.
proof_review.notes: The chapter presents conditional proof templates and a ranked-lock theorem, not a proof of an unspecified concrete concurrent container or every possible resource dependency.

evidence: The central theorem and ranked-lock proof enumerate assumptions and limit the conclusion to linearizability conditions or lock-order cycles respectively.
The coupling, resize, lifecycle, and operation arguments are presented as templates/invariants that a concrete implementation must instantiate.
Race detectors, dynamic lock checks, bounded histories, models, stress, and benchmarks are explicitly prevented from making broader proof claims.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: No universal fairness, starvation freedom, arbitrary-schedule correctness, memory safety, snapshot atomicity, or scalability claim is made from lock count or tool success.

evidence: The standard-library-only Python finite schedule model passed exact nine-line stdout, empty stderr, and zero exit status under the repository verifier.
The model emits evidence=finite_fine_grained_lock_model and reproduces distinct-stripe overlap, same-stripe exclusion, sorted pair order, final mappings, and release.
All eight external destinations returned HTTP 200 and all repository-local links passed chapter validation.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No OS threads, real locks, target memory model, arbitrary schedule/history, race detector, lockdep, fault/cancellation, reclamation, throughput, latency, cache, NUMA, or deployment experiment was run.

conceptual_review.notes: The chapter derives fine-grained locking from abstract conflicts and guard maps, then connects coupling, ranked order, optimistic validation, linearization, structural change, reclamation, liveness, and workload evidence without presenting finer granularity as intrinsically superior.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed stable protection identities, stripe deduplication/order, transitive callback hazards, structured partial-acquisition cleanup, resize generations, aggregate/snapshot semantics, lifecycle/quiescence, race/history/lock-order tools, security skew, and wait/hold/retry/cache/NUMA measurements against a coarse oracle.

pedagogical_review.notes: The review sheet supports retrieval; exposition progresses from conflicts to ownership and proof; ten examples vary across mapping, deadlock, traversal, validation, counters, rotations, resize, snapshots, reclamation, and benchmarking; five exercises progress from definitions to unfamiliar spatial-index transfer with complete answers.

limitations: Internal authoring, primary/official-source, mathematical, bounded executable-model, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical evidence only; no external academic, Herlihy/Wing, Heller et al., Oracle, POSIX, Linux, SEI, concurrency, database, operating-system, security, performance, reliability, or independent practitioner review is claimed.
